metas.note:
Road 970 in the far north, on the border with Norway, is easily recognizable: it runs through a river valley with hills on both sides. The river is visible in many places, usually to the northwest. The birch trees around the road are small and stunted.

NOTE: The Generation 3 coverage on this road was taken in the autumn, meaning that the vegetation looks dead and mostly devoid of leaves.

metas.name: Aaland - Pedestrian Signs
metas.note: Some pedestrian signs on Åland have four stripes, with the exact same design found in Sweden. Beware that many pedestrian signs will still be the typical Finnish design.

metas.name: Aaland - Swedish Language
metas.note: Åland is monolingually Swedish. If you see only Swedish, and no Finnish language, but you suspect that you are in Finland, consider the Åland Islands.

metas.name: Aaland Busstop
metas.note:
Bus stops on Åland include a white plate with 4 numbers. Some also include this semicircle sign on top.

NOTE: Some bus stops in Mariehamn do not follow this rule.

metas.name: Aaland Flag
metas.note: Åland is a group of islands off the southwestern coast. It is an autonomous, mostly self-governing region of Finland with its own flag. Though it has a special status, for country streaks purposes it is still counted as part of Finland.

metas.name: Aaland License Plate
metas.note: Licence plates on Åland are white with blue text, making them appear almost completely white on Street View. They are noticeably quite short and lack the European blue strip on the left side.

metas.name: Blue Street Sign
metas.note: This style of blue street sign with white text is unique to the cities of Seinäjoki and Isokyrö southeast of Vaasa.

metas.name: Farmland
metas.note: Finland has a lot of farmlands, but the majority of them are concentrated near the west and south coast.

metas.name: Gen 3 - Snow
metas.note:
Generation 3 snow coverage is only found in far northwestern Lapland.

NOTE: Be careful: this tip is specifically about regular Generation 3 coverage. Generation 2, 4, and trekker snow coverage can be found elsewhere.

metas.name: Helsinki Bus
metas.note: The buses in and around Helsinki are typically blue-and-white, with a vertical split. Buses elsewhere can have the same colour scheme, so look for one of these logos on the bus.

metas.name: Helsinki Gen 4 Trekker
metas.note:
Downtown Helsinki has a lot of Generation 4 sidewalk trekker coverage.

NOTE: This tip is specifically about Generation 4 trekker coverage. Generation 3 sidewalk trekkers can be found in many other Finnish cities.

metas.name: Helsinki Tram
metas.note:
Helsinki features these unique green-and-yellow trams.

NOTE: Tampere is the only other Finnish city with trams, but they are red instead of green and yellow.

metas.name: Järvenpää Street Sign
metas.note:
The city of Järvenpää uses street signs with this blue-and-grey coat of arms in the top-left corner. The neighbourhood name is also written above the street name.

NOTE: If you see a street sign with a coat of arms not mentioned in this guide, you should be near Kerava or Lahti.

metas.name: Jyväskylä Bus
metas.note: Buses in Jyväskylä are almost completely green.

metas.name: Kerava Street Signs
metas.note: The city of Kerava uses street signs with this blue-and-yellow coat of arms in the top-left corner.

metas.name: Kilpisjärvi Road
metas.note:
Due to its proximity to the Scandinavian Mountains, the area near Kilpisjärvi features a unique hilly landscape, with low vegetation.

NOTE: The Generation 2 coverage on this road was taken during Spring, so the vegetation looks dead.

metas.name: Kuopio Street Sign
metas.note: Notably, Kuopio can use these signs, which use a thicker, more compact font.

metas.name: Lahti Street Signs
metas.note:
Lahti uses these street signs with a black border and all capital letters.

NOTE: You can rarely find similar signs in other cities, but Lahti almost exclusively uses this design. Notably, Kuopio can use these signs, which use a thicker, more compact font.

metas.name: Long Tilted Antenna
metas.note:
This slightly tilted, long antenna can be found in southwestern Finland.

NOTE: Do not mix it up with the straight long antenna.

metas.name: No Antenna
metas.note: Generation 3 coverage with no antenna at all can be found in south-central Finland.

metas.name: Northern Trees
metas.note: Small, stunted trees with spindly, thin trunks are common in northern Finland.

metas.name: Oulu Bus
metas.note: Buses in Oulu have a pink front.

metas.name: Roadnumber - 1
metas.note:
Finnish regional roads have 3- or 4-digit road numbers. The first digit of those road numbers is region-specific. These regions are distributed in a rough south-to-north order, starting from 1 in the south to 9 in the north.

These road numbers often appear on direction signs. Learning the regions can help with cutting down on scanning time for 5k’s, or give you a rough region to plonk in during quick no move games.

NOTE: Major roads with 2-digit road numbers do not adhere to this geographic pattern.

metas.name: Sami language
metas.note: The Sámi languages are spoken in the far north of Finland. In this region, you can sometimes find bilingual signs with place names in both Finnish and Sámi. Unlike Finnish, its alphabet uses the letter c.

metas.name: Swedish Language
metas.note: The Swedish language is common in some coastal areas in the south and the west. In these areas, bilingual Swedish or Finnish texts are common. If you see Swedish language in a Finnish setting, do not guess inland.

metas.name: Tampere Bus
metas.note: The buses in and around Tampere are blue on the bottom and white on the top. The word ‘NYSSE’ is written on the sides of the buses.

metas.name: Tampere Metal Plate
metas.note: You can find these unique metallic plates on houses, lamp posts, and signposts in Tampere.

metas.name: Tampere Tram
metas.note: Tampere is the only other Finnish city with trams (except Helsinki), but they are red instead of green and yellow.

metas.name: Turku Bus
metas.note: Buses in Turku are uniquely yellow, with a white rear.

metas.name: Wind Turbines
metas.note: Wind turbines are most commonly found along the west coast of Finland, with some exceptions.
